title: Cross-engine vector search — 4 engines, one harness
subtitle: MyVector · vsql_vector · pgvector · MariaDB — fashion-mnist-784, published ground truth
nav: cross-engine (full metrics) · MySQL versions · real-dataset by version
description: A cross-engine comparison run through a neutral third-party harness — VillageSQL's vector-dev-bench (the MyVector profile is upstream PR #14). Same real dataset (fashion-mnist-784-euclidean, 60k × 784, L2) and published exact ground truth drive all three engines; this answers "how does MyVector's HNSW compare to VillageSQL's own vsql_vector, pgvector, and MariaDB's native vector indexes on the same workload and harness?" (The other pages compare MyVector across MySQL versions.)
caveats: ⚡ MyVector here is the optimized build (PR #278), re-measured through this neutral harness: this page's MyVector curve is the NEON kernel + keepPrunedConnections build, re-run via VillageSQL's own recall_bench (not MyVector's harness) on the same A2 container. Versus the prior scalar build it lifts recall-per-ef (ef=10 0.944→0.971, ef=20 0.983→0.991 — from keepPrunedConnections densifying the graph) and QPS (+12% at ef=50, +37% at ef=800 — from the vectorized L2 kernel). That the gain reproduces in a third-party harness is the point: it's not an artifact of MyVector's own measurement. (Unmerged, so main is still scalar.)

Harness: VillageSQL vector-dev-bench recall_bench.py — one PyMySQL/psql path, numpy ground truth. The MyVector engine profile is upstream PR #14. It reports build time + a recall@10/QPS ef_search sweep; insert and exact-KNN columns aren't produced by this harness, so they show “—”.
Dataset & recall: fashion-mnist-784-euclidean (60k train × 784-d, 10k test, L2) with recall@10 scored against the dataset's published exact neighbors (ann-benchmarks methodology).

Index params: HNSW M=16, ef_construction=200 for MyVector and pgvector. MariaDB's MHNSW fixes ef_construction at 10 internally (not tunable) — documented, not matched. MariaDB also floors mhnsw_ef_search to ~2×M (≈32), so an ef_search=10 request is not a valid operating point (QPS below the ef=20 point despite less work); that point is omitted from MariaDB's plotted curve (kept in the result JSON under ef_search_excluded). The other engines apply no such floor, so their ef=10 points are plotted as-is.

Cache fairness: each engine's graph sized to stay in memory above the ~188 MB index — MyVector loads its HNSW into its own memory (InnoDB pool 2 GB for the build scan); MariaDB mhnsw_max_cache_size=1 GiB; pgvector shared_buffers=2 GB.
Headline cards are the warm ef_search=200 sweep point, so all three engines are compared at one operating point.
Hardware: all three on the same A2 host (8 vCPU / 24 GB), each container pinned to 4 vCPU / 16 GB.
